text.title: North Star Metric Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every North Star Metric application MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The NSM MUST count occurrences of the moment a customer receives the product's core value (a usage or outcome event: messages sent inside teams, nights booked, projects completed, reports delivered). Revenue, MRR, signups, registered users, pageviews, sessions and undifferentiated MAU MUST NOT be the NSM; revenue may appear only as the outcome the NSM is validated against.

rationale.source: Sean Ellis and Morgan Brown, Hacking Growth (2017), chapter on the North Star Metric; Amplitude, The North Star Playbook (John Cutler and Bruce McCarthy, 2019)

rule.rationale: Revenue lags value by months and cannot be moved by the people who ship the product this week; signups can be bought. Airbnb's nights booked, Slack's messages sent within teams and Facebook's active users are all counts of value exchanged, which is why they moved before revenue did. A team told to grow "MRR" optimises price and packaging; a team told to grow "weekly teams completing a project" optimises the product.

rule.statement: The definition slot MUST name the exact event or events counted, the unit (users, accounts, teams, transactions), the time window (daily, weekly, 28-day) and the inclusion and exclusion conditions (internal accounts, free vs paid, test data, minimum threshold), such that two analysts querying the warehouse independently return the same number. A dashboard URL where the current value is published MUST be present.

rationale.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook (2019); widely established practice in product analytics

rule.rationale: "Weekly active teams" means five different numbers until someone writes down whether a team is active at one message or at ten and whether the 200 internal test workspaces are excluded. Ambiguous NSMs are silently redefined by whoever pulls the number for the board, and the metric loses its alignment function the first time two decks disagree.

rule.statement: The decision record MUST list at least three candidate metrics and score each against the same five criteria: expresses customer value, is a leading indicator of revenue, is actionable by product and marketing teams within a quarter, is understandable without a data team, and is measurable today from existing events. The chosen NSM MUST be the highest-scoring candidate or the record MUST state why it is not.

rationale.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook (2019), NSM checklist; Reforge, North Star Metric selection

rule.rationale: An NSM chosen by the loudest executive is the misalignment problem restated with a name. The scored table is what lets marketing, product and sales see that "signups" lost on the leading-indicator criterion and "revenue" lost on actionability, so the eventual choice is defended by shared criteria rather than by authority.

rule.statement: Before adoption the record MUST show a cohort analysis on the product's own data demonstrating that users or accounts above the NSM threshold retain (or convert to paid) at a materially higher rate than those below it, with the cohort size, the period and the retention delta stated. An NSM asserted to "correlate with retention" without the numbers MUST NOT be adopted; the validation section of the definition sheet is filled with yes / no / inconclusive and the date of the run.

rationale.source: Sean Ellis and Morgan Brown, Hacking Growth (2017); Amplitude, The North Star Playbook (2019), leading-indicator validation

rule.rationale: The NSM's whole claim is that moving it moves revenue later. Facebook's "7 friends in 10 days" and Slack's "2,000 messages" were cohort findings, not slogans. An unvalidated NSM can be moved for two quarters (more notifications, more nudges) while retention stays flat, and by then every OKR in the company is attached to it.

rule.statement: Exactly one NSM MUST be adopted per product. The record MUST NOT define "two North Stars" or a primary plus a secondary; every runner-up is either an input metric under the NSM or a rejected candidate with its rejection reason stated.

rationale.source: Sean Ellis, North Star Metric concept; Amplitude, The North Star Playbook (2019)

rule.rationale: Two North Stars recreate the original problem: marketing takes one, product takes the other, and trade-offs between them are resolved politically. The metric exists to be the tiebreaker; a tiebreaker that needs a tiebreaker is decoration.

rule.statement: The NSM MUST be decomposed into three to five input metrics that together drive it (typically along breadth, depth, frequency and efficiency), each with an owning team, a current value and a target. Every input MUST be one that its owning team can move within a quarter through its own work; an input nobody owns or nobody can move is removed from the tree.

rationale.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook (2019), inputs framework (breadth, depth, frequency, efficiency)

rule.rationale: The NSM is a lagging aggregate of everyone's work and no single team can move it directly. The input tree is where alignment actually happens: growth owns breadth (new active teams), product owns depth (projects per team), lifecycle owns frequency. Without it, "grow the NSM" becomes each team's private interpretation, which is the misalignment the methodology was invoked to fix.

rule.statement: The record MUST state at least one way the chosen NSM could be inflated without delivering value (paid signups, notification spam, counting internal or bot activity, lowering the threshold) and the guard for each (exclusion in the definition, a paired quality or retention metric, a threshold review rule). An NSM that a single team can inflate with spend alone MUST be rejected under r-nsm-counts-value-delivered.

rationale.source: Goodhart's law (Charles Goodhart, 1975; formulation by Marilyn Strathern, 1997); widely established practice in metric design

rule.rationale: Any number that decides bonuses and roadmaps will be gamed; the only question is whether the record anticipated it. "Messages sent" inflates with bot integrations, "active accounts" inflates with a one-click reactivation email, and every one of these produces a rising chart, a flat retention curve and a quarter of misdirected effort.

rule.statement: The NSM and its definition MUST NOT be changed silently. Any change to the counted event, unit, window, threshold or inclusion rule requires a new decision record that links the previous one, restates the validation under r-nsm-validated-against-retention and records the date from which the two series are not comparable. The current NSM MUST be reviewed against its retention and revenue link at least once per year and the review date recorded.

rationale.source: Amplitude, The North Star Playbook (2019), on NSM stability; widely established practice in decision records (Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions, 2011)

rule.rationale: A metric that the company steers by is a time series; redefining it without a break marker turns two years of history into noise and lets a redefinition masquerade as growth. Redefinitions also happen for the wrong reasons (the old number stopped going up), which the linked record makes visible.

section.title: Conclusion targets used by the decision tree

rule.statement: Run the full procedure; emit an artefact passing the output contract.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when the NSM signals hold.

rule.statement: Skip; surface the missing precondition; do not synthesize.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when there is no event data to validate an NSM against.
